activity: to explain why the Roman Empire split and fell using a map of its borders
knowledge_domain: to explain why the Roman Empire split and fell using a map of its borders
fact: In March 1936, Hitler sent German troops into the Rhineland, breaking the Treaty of Versailles, and Britain and France did not use force to stop him.
story:
Hazel spread Grandpa's enormous atlas across the kitchen table so fast that it knocked over the salt shaker, and Nutmeg the cat bolted from the room like a gray turbine spinning out of control. On Monday she had to explain to her whole class why the Roman Empire split in two and then fell, and everyone said use the map, but nobody said how. The empire's borders sprawled across the paper like a giant octopus, and she needed to make it make sense.

"Do you want tea while you stare at that thing?" Grandpa asked. "You look like you're trying to digest the whole empire."

"I'm digesting the borders," Hazel said, tapping the squiggly lines. "Rome got too big to guard, so they split it in half, east and west. Then barbarian groups pushed in from outside the borders." She frowned. "But why did the pushes work? Rome had a huge army."

Grandpa just shrugged and went back to his crossword, which was his way of saying figure it out yourself. Hazel leaned close to the map. The paper smelled like dust and old coffee, and the afternoon light through the window made the yellowed page almost luminous. Then she remembered something from the library book she'd read last week.

In her mind she was back in the library's squishy orange chair, reading about March 1936, when Hitler sent German troops into the Rhineland. That broke the Treaty of Versailles, and she had stared at that sentence so long the librarian asked if she was asleep. The book said Britain and France did not use force to stop him. Nobody stopped the first rule-break. Hazel sat bolt upright at the kitchen table. That was it. The first push into Roman land had gone unanswered, so the tribes along the borders pushed harder, again and again, until the whole western half came apart. It was like when Dario swiped one of Ms. Pratt's dry-erase markers in October and nothing happened, so in November he tried to swipe the whole projector.

"Grandpa, I've got it!" she shouted. "Nobody stopped the first push, so there were bigger ones, and Rome broke!" She grabbed a red marker and traced the borders, then drew fat arrows crashing through them from the outside.

"Well," Grandpa said, peering over his glasses, "please don't arrow my atlas to pieces before dinner."

Hazel grinned and held the marker over the western half like a tiny Roman emperor deciding its fate. "Too late. The western empire falls first, right here."

activity: recovering from a cold or flu at home
knowledge_domain: recovering from a cold or flu at home
fact: According to the U.S. CDC, adults catch an average of two to three colds a year, and children often catch more.
story:
On the third day of sneezing, Vincent dragged his blanket out to Grandpa's sunporch, where the wood floor seemed to radiate heat even in November. This was his third cold since school started, and he was keeping count, because three felt like a personal failure.

"Three," he muttered into his tissue. "Nobody else gets three."

Grandpa was folded into the wicker chair with a crossword, in no hurry at all, doing the puzzle at his leisure. "Three what?"

"Colds. Since fall. Am I broken or something?"

Grandpa tapped his pencil against his knee. "Hm. Is three a lot? What's your evidence?"

Vincent thought about it. Devon had one cold. Maya had two, maybe. But then, Devon's little sister seemed to have a runny nose every single week, forever. And the kindergarten wing at school sounded like a foghorn convention in December. Maybe three wasn't weird for kids. Maybe adults were just quieter about their sniffles.

"Grandpa, how many colds do you get in a year?"

"Two. Sometimes three." Grandpa filled in a word. "And I'm a grown man, so that's normal for grown-ups."

Vincent sat up straighter, blanket sliding off one shoulder. So if adults averaged two or three colds a year, and little kids caught them even more often than that, then three colds since fall for a ten-year-old was practically ordinary. Not broken. Just a kid being a kid. He felt like he'd solved a case with only the foghorn wing and Devon's sniffling sister as clues.

He tested it anyway. At dinner, he asked Grandma, and she said, "Three or four some years, and your mother caught even more than that when she was your age." Case closed.

The next morning Vincent put the thermometer back in the drawer without checking it, carried his cereal out to the sunporch, and declared, "Grandpa, I'm taking my recovery at leisure. Like you."

"Radical idea," Grandpa said, and handed him half the crossword.

activity: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
knowledge_domain: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
fact: Airplane mode turns off a phone's radio signals, including the cellular connection it uses for calls and texts.
story:
Sophie's new phone sat in her pocket all through math, heavy as a secret. Mrs. Ruiz kept a basket by the door for phones, and nobody argued, because she had a monopoly on the rules in room 12 and everyone knew it. At lunch Sophie finally took the phone out. Her mother had promised to text the pickup plan before the class trip meeting at 2:45, because if Sophie missed the bus, nobody would be home until six. The screen showed nothing. No texts. No little envelope. She checked the number her mother had typed into the contacts list, and it was right.

At the next desk, Marcus leaned over. "My mom texted me twice already," he said. "Field trip's still on. My phone's been buzzing all day." He shook his pocket, and it buzzed again on cue. Sophie looked at her own screen. The bars in the corner were gone, and in their place a tiny airplane. She had pressed things the night before, hunting for the flashlight, and she remembered tapping an icon that looked like a plane.

"Airplane mode," Marcus said, reading over her shoulder. "My dad leaves it on by accident all the time."

Sophie thought about that. The plane icon must mean something was off. She opened settings, found the airplane button, and tapped it gray. The little plane vanished, the screen paused, and then the bars climbed back. Three messages dropped in at once, one on top of another, so fast the screen seemed to saturate with them before her eyes. The first was her mother: Bus leaves at 3:15, not 3:45. Meet by the doors at 3:10.

Sophie typed back, Got it, and slid the phone into the basket as Mrs. Ruiz called for attention. Marcus whispered, "That was basically the equivalent of your phone being asleep with its ears plugged."

"It was off," Sophie said. "The whole time."

activity: to mediate an argument between two friends without taking a side
knowledge_domain: to mediate an argument between two friends without taking a side
fact: Mediators usually start by setting ground rules, such as one person speaks at a time and no name-calling, which both sides agree to before talking.
story:
The shouting reached the kitchen before Levi's friends did. Marcus and Dara had been best friends since kindergarten, but today they stormed through Grandpa's screen door arguing about a birdhouse they had built together for the school fair.

"You sanded it crooked on purpose," Marcus said.

"Your paint job looks like a raccoon did it," Dara shot back.

Levi had promised his grandpa he would handle this himself, because Grandpa said arguing friends were "good practice." Practice for what, Levi didn't know yet, but he had a cookie riding on it.

"Okay, okay," Levi said, holding up both hands. "Dara, tell me your side."

Dara talked. Then Marcus talked. Then Dara interrupted, Marcus called her "Birdhouse Bandit," and the whole argument restarted, louder than before. Levi tried again, letting each of them vent about sanding and painting. This time Dara called Marcus a "Hammer Klutz," and the fight blew up a second time, complete with a dramatic fling of sandpaper.

Levi sat down on the porch steps and thought. Both times, the fight had restarted the moment someone interrupted or threw an insult. The problem wasn't the birdhouse at all. The problem was the way they were talking. Maybe the conversation itself needed rules.

He stood up. "Before we go again, we need ground rules," he announced. "One person speaks at a time, and no name-calling. Both of you have to agree to them before you talk."

Marcus squinted. "That's not a real thing."

"It is now," Levi said. "Do you agree?"

"Fine," said Dara.

"Fine," said Marcus, though he said it like the word had hurt him.

With the rules in place, they took turns, and something strange happened. Marcus admitted the paint looked better than he'd expected. Dara admitted the sanding was, in her words, "mostly competent." They even negotiated: Dara would accommodate Marcus by adding a second perch, if Marcus let her carve her name under the roof.

Grandpa came out with the census forms he'd been filling out and three cookies on a plate. "Who won?"

"Nobody," said Levi. "That's the trick."

Grandpa peered at the birdhouse. "Twelve votes for the mediator," he said, handing Levi two cookies.

activity: to explain supply and demand using the price of strawberries in summer and winter
knowledge_domain: to explain supply and demand using the price of strawberries in summer and winter
fact: When unpaid interest is added to a debt, the next month's interest is charged on that interest too, so the debt grows faster over time.
story:
Grandpa kept a price notebook, which Jessica thought was the most retired thing a person could do. Every Saturday he wrote down what strawberries cost at the farm stand, and he let her come along to do the writing. In June the berries were two dollars a basket, fat and red and stacked in pyramids. By late July the stand had tables and tables of them, baskets spilling over, and the sign said a dollar fifty. "Write it down exactly," Grandpa said. "The truth doesn't care how we feel about it."

Jessica's cousin Dana was there too, sulking on the porch with a letter from a card company. "I stopped using it in April," Dana said. "How is the balance bigger than it was in May?" Jessica was working on an answer to that, sort of, because Grandpa had offered her a deal: figure out both mysteries, the strawberries and the debt, and he would fund a strawberry shortcake with the summer-cheap berries. A shortcake was a real, edible reason to think.

The strawberry half she got first. More berries at the stand meant the farmer dropped the price to move them all; in winter, when the fields were frozen and basically extinct until spring, a basket cost five dollars because almost nobody had any. Nobody could see the invisible rule doing it. You only saw prices. Grandpa had pointed at the empty winter field last December and said, "There's your teacher," which was typical Grandpa.

Dana's problem was trickier because the letter just showed a bigger number, no reasons. Jessica asked to see the older statements, and Dana dug them out of her backpack in the guest room, where the window was drafty even in July because the old house had single-pane glass and nobody had gotten around to fixing the insulation. Jessica laid the statements in a row like strawberry baskets. May, June, July. The balance grew a little each month even though Dana had bought nothing with it since April.

"So the interest they charge gets added to what you owe," Jessica said slowly, watching the numbers line up, "and then next month they charge interest on that too. On the interest." Dana stared at the row of statements. "That's why it's going up faster than I pay it down." Jessica nodded. It was like the strawberry rule, another invisible thing you could only see by its footprints.

The shortcake happened on Sunday, built from dollar-fifty berries and Grandpa's heavy alloy mixing bowl, the one that had survived three decades of dropping. Dana brought her statements to the table and announced she was paying the whole balance off before August. Grandpa served the berries and said, "Winter prices are coming, one way or another." Jessica took the biggest slice.

activity: to explain supply and demand using the price of strawberries in summer and winter
knowledge_domain: to explain supply and demand using the price of strawberries in summer and winter
fact: Simple interest is paid only on the original amount deposited, called the principal, so it adds the same dollar amount every year.
story:
Zoe had been saving for a new bike since September, and today the bank statement finally arrived. She tore it open right there in the lobby, because waiting until she got home seemed like a punishment nobody had ordered. Her grandfather, who had driven her, was busy arguing with a teller about a fee, so Zoe sat down on the granite bench by the window, the one freckled with gray lichen, and spread the statements from the last three years across her knees.

Something was wrong. Or something was weird, which at Zoe's house amounted to nearly the same thing. She had put in one hundred dollars when she opened the account. The first year, the bank added three dollars. She'd expected the second year to be bigger, because now she had one hundred and three dollars earning money. It wasn't. It was three dollars again. Same the third year. Exactly three dollars, every single time, like a bird that refused to learn a new song.

"You look like you're solving a crime," her grandfather said, dropping onto the bench beside her. He was still holding his fee argument like a dog holding a bone, clearly planning to recount it to the teller's manager.

"It added three dollars every year. Exactly three." She showed him the statements. "Why doesn't it grow? Strawberries grow. That's my project for school, explaining strawberries. In June they're two dollars a basket because everybody's got them, and in January they're six because nobody does. More of something, price goes down. Less of something, price goes up. That part makes sense. This doesn't."

Her grandfather tapped the top statement with one finger. "That's simple interest. It's paid only on the original amount you deposited. The original amount is called the principal." He stood up, straightened his jacket, and went back to battle with the teller, leaving Zoe staring at the word on the page.

So it wasn't broken. It wasn't even stubborn, exactly, though "obstinate" was the word she'd put in her vocabulary list last week and this seemed like a fine place to use it. The interest only looked at the hundred dollars, never at the extra three, never at the pile that came after. Zoe did the math on the back of the envelope: one hundred, one hundred three, one hundred six, one hundred nine. A staircase with steps exactly the same height, going up and up at three dollars a year, while her bike sat in the shop window, unimpressed.

She folded the statements, walked to the counter beside her grandfather, and slid her papers toward the teller. "Excuse me," she said. "Is there an account where the interest isn't like this one?"

activity: to fast, pray or keep a day of rest for part of a day as their family does and explain why
knowledge_domain: to fast, pray or keep a day of rest for part of a day as their family does and explain why
fact: The Yom Kippur fast lasts about 25 hours, from sunset one day until after nightfall the next.
story:
Victor had eaten his fill at Grandma's table an hour before sunset, because tonight was the start of Yom Kippur and he had decided, for the first time, that he was going to try the whole fast. Not just until lunch. The whole thing.

"How long is it, really?" he asked Grandpa, who was filling a water pitcher and then setting it far back on the counter, out of reach.

"From sunset tonight until after nightfall tomorrow," Grandpa said. "About twenty-five hours."

Victor frowned. "Twenty-five? A day is twenty-four."

"Count it yourself," Grandpa said, and went to light the holiday candles.

So Victor did count, lying on the guest room bed with the closet light off and the house gone quiet the way it only got at Grandpa's. Sunset at 6:41 tonight. He did the math on the back of a receipt from the drugstore. Twenty-four hours would end at 6:41 tomorrow evening, but the sky would still hold light then. The fast went on until the sky let go of it completely, past 7:40. An extra hour, wearing darkness like a coat.

The problem arrived the next afternoon, at hour twenty. His head ached and the smell of Grandma's honey cake, prepared and waiting in the kitchen, drifted down the hall like a personal insult. He found Grandpa on the porch and made his offer. "Compromise. I break it an hour early. Nobody has to know."

Grandpa looked at the trees. "Last year your cousin Ben tried it your way. He hid in the bathroom at hour twenty and ate a granola bar. He still talks about it, like it's a scar." He turned his palm up, empty. "The fast isn't mandatory for you yet. You're not thirteen. You chose this."

"That's the problem," Victor said. "I chose it."

He had assumed a day of rest meant a day of doing nothing, but sitting still made the hunger louder, so he tested a simple idea: if being busy beat being hungry, then work was rest. He helped Grandma sweep the porch, carried the chairs out for the meal, read two chapters of a book aloud to her while she peeled nothing, cooked nothing, tasted nothing. The hour that had seemed impossible slid past.

Outside, the sky went from orange to gray to ink. Grandpa stood at the window, watching the last light drain off the neighbor's roof, and Victor stood beside him, counting without numbers.

"There," Grandpa said at last. "Nightfall."

Grandma carried out bread and water, and Victor reached for it.

activity: performing on stage for the first time in a school concert
knowledge_domain: performing on stage for the first time in a school concert
fact: The squeal of microphone feedback happens when sound from a loudspeaker goes back into the microphone, gets amplified again, and loops louder and louder.
story:
Alexandra stood in the wings of the school auditorium, holding her violin like it might bolt for the exit. Her mother had said stage fright wasn't hereditary, since Grandma apparently once sang a solo in front of four hundred people without fainting, but Alexandra suspected her knees hadn't inherited that gene. The principal, Ms. Okafor, was at the podium reading a citation for the music program, some long list of awards, and then it was time for the sound check. Alexandra was first.

She walked out, and the moment the microphone stand was set in front of her, a whistle tore through the auditorium, so piercing that kids in the third row covered their ears. Ms. Okafor winced and switched the mic off. "We'll try again in a minute," she called, but her voice was tight, and Alexandra could tell she was worried. The concert was in an hour, and every performer needed the mic tested.

Alexandra stared at the loudspeaker standing on the stage floor behind the microphone, then at the mic itself, then back again. She remembered how the whistle had swelled, louder and louder, like something feeding itself. Sound from that speaker, she thought, going straight back into the mic, getting amplified again, then back out the speaker, around and around, louder every loop. It was like a rumor growing each time it was repeated.

She decided to simulate the real concert instead of a timid little check. "Can we turn everything on?" she asked the sound helper, a sixth grader named Theo. "But I want to stand here, sideways, with the mic pointed away from the speaker." She angled the stand so the microphone faced the empty front rows and turned her shoulder to block the line between them. Theo flipped the switch. The speaker hummed to life. No whistle.

"Try talking," Theo said.

"Testing," Alexandra said, and the word came out clean and round through the speaker, no squeal at all. Theo gave her a thumbs up, and Ms. Okafor, watching from the third row, let out a breath and smiled. Then she waved the next performer over, and Alexandra, her violin tucked under her chin, drew her bow across the first bright, steady note.

activity: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
knowledge_domain: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
fact: Coping means the ways a person handles stress or difficult feelings; healthy coping strategies include exercise, getting enough sleep and talking with someone trusted.
story:
The waiting room clock said 3:02, and Zoey had to be at band practice by 3:45, which gave the whole morning a squeezed, ticking feeling. She sat with her knees perpendicular to the floor, heels hooked on the chair leg, and reread the note her best friend Priya had slipped into her locker that morning. "Bad day. Lunch disaster. Mom working late again. Come find me before practice." Zoey had no idea what to write back, so she'd shoved it in her pocket and taken it out four times since.

She was here because of the stomachaches. Every Sunday night for a month, like clockwork, and then gone by Tuesday. That was the part that didn't make sense. She'd started keeping a list on her phone, and when she looked at the dates, a pattern jumped out: bad stomach, no sleep the night before. Sunday nights she lay awake until one, sometimes two. Monday nights she slept fine. She had a theory, and today she planned to test it by telling the doctor everything, straight out, before the clock hit 3:20.

Outside the window, a strip of hospital garden buzzed with bees that pollinated the rows of purple flowers, moving flower to flower like they had their own deadline. A poster near the fish tank read FEELING STRESSED? YOU'RE NOT ALONE. A man across from her read a magazine, and a little boy built a tower of blocks and knocked it down, over and over.

When the nurse called her name, Zoey unfolded her list. She told the doctor about the pattern, the Sundays, the sleepless nights. The doctor nodded slowly. "What you're describing sounds like anxiety," she said. "Stress that the body holds onto." Zoey's stomach flipped, but not in the bad way. A hidden cause, and it had a name.

"Coping," the doctor said. "It means the ways a person handles stress or hard feelings. Some ways are healthier than others."

On the drive to practice, Zoey texted Priya: "Exercise helps. Sleep helps. Talking helps. I'm testing all three. You first. What do you do after a bad day?"

Priya's reply came before Zoey reached the gym: "Hide in my room. Why?"

"New plan," Zoey typed, pushing through the doors. "Meet me at the track at 3:45."

activity: to fast, pray or keep a day of rest for part of a day as their family does and explain why
knowledge_domain: to fast, pray or keep a day of rest for part of a day as their family does and explain why
fact: Jewish views of the afterlife vary widely: Orthodox Judaism holds to a future resurrection of the dead, while Reform Judaism puts more weight on how people live now.
story:
Hailey had decided to try keeping Shabbat from Friday sundown to Saturday noon, the way her family did, even though her best friends were all at the pool by ten. In the kitchen, the last thing she did before sunset was tape a note over the light switch, because her mother said the rule was no electricity, and Hailey wanted to be systematic about it. No phone, no TV, no turning things on. She set a loaf of challah on the table and waited in the dimming light, wondering what would actually be different.

Saturday morning she sat at the same table with her two cousins, Maya and Dov, who had come for lunch. Bored already, Hailey asked the question she'd been carrying around for weeks: "What happens after you die?"

"Orthodox Jews believe there'll be a resurrection of the dead," Dov said, tearing his bread. "Like, actually, in the future. Bodies rising."

Maya shrugged. "At our synagogue, our rabbi says what matters is how you live now. That's the whole point."

"They can't both be right," Hailey said.

"Why not?" Maya said. "Nobody's seen it. It's not like you can check."

That stopped Hailey. She looked at the covered switch, the silent phone in the drawer, the candles burnt down to stubs. She couldn't see whether resting had changed anything inside her either, but she had a way to test it. She had gone all morning without checking her phone once, which had never happened on a normal Saturday, and she had noticed the smell of the bread and the sound of Dov chewing, small things the screen usually magnified into the only things in the room.

She thought about last winter, when she'd skipped her grandmother's shiva because a swim meet mattered more to her, and how she still couldn't decide if that had been a mistake or just a choice.

"Okay," she said at last. "Different answers to the same question. Maybe that's allowed."

Maya stole a piece of Hailey's challah and grinned. "Maybe that's the most Jewish answer of all."

Dov reached for the butter dish and knocked over the candle stub, and all three of them scrambled to catch it before it rolled off the table.

activity: to walk to the corner store alone, buy milk and count the change
knowledge_domain: to walk to the corner store alone, buy milk and count the change
fact: Washing your hands before touching a cut helps keep germs from getting into the wound.
story:
Samuel stood at the counter with his mother's five dollar bill folded in his fist like a secret. "You can supervise from the porch," she said, "but you're doing it yourself. Milk, and bring me the change." From the porch she watched him march down the walk, and Samuel pretended not to notice, though he stood a little straighter anyway.

At Marta's Corner Market he found the milk, cold and sweating, and carried it to the register with both hands. Marta rang it up, took his five, and handed him a quarter, a dime, and two pennies. Samuel stepped aside, laid the coins on the edge of the counter, and counted. He counted again. If the milk was $4.56, he was owed forty-four cents, and thirty-seven cents was not forty-four cents. Either he was wrong or she was, and he did not think he was wrong, because he had done the subtraction twice in his head while walking past the blue house with the influential yellow mailbox, the one everybody in the neighborhood used when giving directions. "Excuse me," he said, holding up the coins. "I think I'm short seven cents." Marta squinted at the register, said, "The button sticks on the fours," and dropped a nickel and two pennies into his palm.

He was still grinning about that when he got home and found his little cousin Theo on the back steps, knee bleeding in a long red smear, sniffling. "I fell off the wagon," Theo said, which was his whole diagnosis and clearly enough for him. Samuel set the milk on the kitchen table and reached for Theo's knee, then stopped. Last year the school nurse had helped Samuel with a gashed palm, and the first thing she had done, before anything else, was walk to the sink and wash her hands. He had thought it was strange then, but now it clicked into place like the change problem: something you did before the touching, not after. Germs didn't get into the cut if they never got onto the hands that touched the cut.

"Wait right there," Samuel said. "I have to wash my hands first." Theo looked at him like he was crazy. "My knee is the problem, not your hands." "My hands are going to land on your knee," Samuel said, soaping up to the wrists, "so they're part of the problem now." Theo thought about that, frowned, and held still while Samuel rinsed, dried, and pressed a clean paper towel against the scrape.

Samuel carried the milk to his mother along with the exact change, forty-four cents, counted twice. She looked at the coins, then at Theo's bandaged knee, then at Samuel's still-damp hands. "Forty-four cents and one fixed cousin," she said. "Not bad for a first trip." Theo lifted his leg into the light to admire it. "He washed his hands before he even touched me," he announced. "Like a doctor."

activity: recovering from a cold or flu at home
knowledge_domain: recovering from a cold or flu at home
fact: A stuffy nose during a cold is caused mainly by swollen blood vessels and inflamed tissue in the lining of the nose, not only by a buildup of mucus.
story:
Jaxson sat at the kitchen table with a wastebasket between his knees and the family's last box of tissues in front of him, so depleted it held only four. He had blown his nose eleven times since breakfast, hard, the way you would to clear out anything clogged, and after every single blow his nose still felt packed shut, like a sock stuck in a doorway.

"Stop blowing so much," said his older sister, Priya, dumping soup into a pot. "You're going to make your ears pop."

"It's already blocked. Blowing is supposed to fix that." He folded the tissue, blew again, and listened. Nothing moved. He pinched his nostrils closed and breathed in through his mouth, then slowly released them, and there was still that stuffed, thick feeling, deep in there, where no tissue could reach. That was strange. If mucus were the problem, blowing should have cleared some of it. He grabbed the house tablet and typed why does blowing not help a stuffy nose.

The first answer stopped him cold. A stuffy nose during a cold is caused mainly by swollen blood vessels and inflamed tissue in the lining of the nose, not only by a buildup of mucus. He read it twice. So the blockage was puffy, swollen walls, not a pile of gunk. Blowing at swollen walls was like trying to unclog a straw by sucking on it when the straw itself was pinched.

He tried an idea. He ran a towel under hot water, wrung it out, and held it warm against the bridge of his nose for a few minutes, then breathed slowly through each side. When he lowered the towel, air actually moved. Not perfectly, but moved.

"Did you just nominate yourself chief of home medicine?" Priya asked, stirring.

"No. I changed my mind about the tissues. We don't need to buy six boxes. It's not a mucus problem." He slid the nearly empty box across the table to her. "Also, I decided the cold is not a monarchy. Nobody rules it. It just does whatever it wants."

"Poor kingdom," Priya said. "Impoverished, with four tissues left."

Jaxson laughed, then winced, then breathed in, one nostril at a time, counting. "Three," he said. "Four. It's opening up."

activity: to explain why ancient Egyptians built the pyramids and how the Nile shaped their farming
knowledge_domain: to explain why ancient Egyptians built the pyramids and how the Nile shaped their farming
fact: The Panic of 1837 caused a long economic depression in the United States, and many ruined farmers later headed west looking for cheap, fertile land.
story:
Hudson had a report due Monday on why ancient Egyptians built the pyramids, which would have been fine if the exhibit he needed hadn't been closed for cleaning. A paper sign, unbothered by his opinion, said so.

"Gift shop's open," said his little sister Priya, who had come along for the air conditioning and wanted a replica canopic jar she'd been guarding with her eyes since noon.

The museum guide, sweeping near the barrier, tipped her head toward a corridor. "Pioneer wing's open. There's a river model down there too. Sometimes the river helps with the Egypt questions."

Hudson doubted a covered wagon could explain a pyramid, but he followed the corridor anyway. He found a long table with water and silt, a model of the Nile flooding its banks, and a wall panel about fields turning green every year while the desert stayed brown. He pushed a wooden lever and watched the water rise, leave dark mud, then sink. The river was the signal, he thought, the thing farmers watched to know when to plant. That's why priests studied the flood, and why the pharaoh, whose pyramid sat above the sand like a promise, got credit when the harvest came in. Priya pressed the lever too, twice, just to see the mud decompose into the water like cocoa in milk.

Beyond the river table sat a glass case with a diary from 1837. Hudson read the line out loud because it stopped him. "The bank took the farm in the spring. We hear land out west is cheap and the soil is black as coal, so we will risk the trail."

"So they just left?" Priya asked.

"The Panic of 1837 ruined a lot of farmers," Hudson said slowly, connecting it. "Then they went west for the good land." Ruined farmers, black soil, a dangerous trail. People following a signal of their own.

Priya tugged his sleeve. "You owe me a jar."

He bought her the small one, not the big one. She held it up to the light, decided it was better anyway, and marched out the door ahead of him.

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: Gleaning is an ancient practice: the Book of Leviticus in the Hebrew Bible tells farmers to leave the edges of their fields unharvested for the poor and for strangers.
story:
The food bank shared a parking lot with the neighborhood cleanup, so Emily ended up doing both, hauling a bag of trash in one hand and a box of dented soup cans in the other. Inside the food bank, her job was sorting, which mostly meant excavating the bottom of a donation barrel to see what had been squashed flat back in March. That was where she found the envelope.

"Mail goes in the office," said Mr. Alvarez, a volunteer whose grandkid had dragged him along. Then he squinted at it. "Actually, that's addressed to us."

The letter was from a farm two towns over. The handwriting slanted uphill. "You called about surplus kale. Come Saturday and glean the back field. Whatever's left after the harvest is yours." Emily read it twice. "Glean" sounded like something you did to a fish.

"It's an old idea," Mr. Alvarez said. "My grandmother would say it. The Book of Leviticus tells farmers to leave the edges of their fields unharvested, for the poor and for strangers." He handed the letter back. "Never thought I'd see it in a note about kale."

Saturday, Emily rode along in the food bank van. The farmer, a woman named Dot, walked them past rows already picked clean, then stopped at the field's edge, where a fringe of kale and stray cabbage still stood. "Combines can't get this close to the fence," she said. "So it rots. Seems bizarre, all this waste two feet from hunger." Emily tested the idea with her fingers, snapping stem after stem, filling crate after crate. Forty pounds, the scale said at the end.

Dot signed the donation slip and read it over. "Funny thing. I got a letter from the food bank last spring asking for surplus. I never called them back." She looked at Emily. "You all got a letter from me, though. Mine." Emily pulled the envelope from her jacket. The date on the letter was three years old. Somewhere in that donation barrel, buried under soup, an old invitation had waited for the barrel to be dug out. "We'd better answer it," Emily said, and asked Dot for a pen.

activity: to shade a sphere with a light source to show highlight, shadow and cast shadow
knowledge_domain: to shade a sphere with a light source to show highlight, shadow and cast shadow
fact: Reflected light is light bouncing back from the table onto a sphere's shadow side; it is lighter than the core shadow but always darker than the lit side.
story:
Mia stood in front of a painting of an orange with a single lamp shining on it, sketchbook clamped under her arm. She had come to the gallery because her art club's sketching day was mandatory, and because she wanted one thing: to make her drawings stop looking flat. She picked a spot on the bench, opened to a blank page, and drew a circle. Then came the hard part. Where exactly did the light go, and where did the dark?

She shaded one side of the sphere, leaving a bright spot where the lamp would hit it. Behind it she dragged a smudge of graphite for the cast shadow on the table. Then, to make the ball look round, she erased a pale curve along the bottom of the dark side. She held the sketchpad out at arm's length and squinted.

A boy on the next bench leaned over. "Why does yours look like it has two lamps?"

Mia looked again. He was right. The pale curve at the bottom glowed almost white, like a second light hidden under the table. "It's not supposed to be that bright," she muttered. She studied the painting on the wall instead. On the orange's dark side, near the bottom, there was a soft lightness, lighter than the deepest part of the shadow, but never as light as the sunlit side. She tested it: she darkened her pale curve two pencil steps, keeping the core of the shadow darkest of all and the lit side still the brightest.

"Better," the boy said. "It looks like it's sitting on something."

"It's the table bouncing light back up," Mia said. "You just can't let it win."

She decided to isolate that one strip of reflected light and practice it on a second sphere, then a third, building her values in order, brightest to darkest, like a hierarchy. Her eraser was nearly a stub by the time the guard announced closing. Mia packed up slowly, then turned back for one last look at the orange.

"Same model tomorrow," she told it.

activity: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
knowledge_domain: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
fact: A single sentence can mix both: in 'The new park, which cost two million dollars, is a waste,' the cost can be checked but 'a waste' is an opinion.
story:
Colton's phone buzzed at 6:47 on Tuesday, right as he sat down to spaghetti. The skate park group chat had gone from three messages a day to forty, because someone had pasted a letter from the local paper.

The letter said the town should never have agreed to install the skate park behind the elementary school, and it ended with a sentence Colton read four times: "The new park, which cost two million dollars, is a waste." His dad leaned over his shoulder, fork in hand. "Half of that sentence you could check," Dad said, and went back to his pasta.

Colton scrolled. Ravi had written "SO TRUE what a waste of money!!" and Marisol had written "no way, the park is awesome," and then the two of them had started typing in all caps about whose fault it was. Nobody had typed anything about the two million dollars.

He put his fork down. He could not see the town's bank account from the dinner table, but a cost was the kind of thing somebody had to have written down. The Parks Department had a website. He found a page about the skate park, and there it was, a citation at the bottom pointing to the town budget, and the budget said two million dollars. So that half of the sentence was true, or at least checkable, which was not the same as agreeing with it.

But "a waste" was different. He stared at the two words. Ravi thought the money should have gone to a pool. Marisol thought the park was the best thing in town. There was no budget page for awesome. His little sister wandered through the kitchen and he asked her, out of pure curiosity, whether she thought the park was a waste. "It's where I learned to drop in," she said, and took a garlic bread stick with her.

Back in the chat, Colton typed slowly, then faster: "Two different things got mixed in one sentence. The two million dollars part checks out, I found it in the town budget. The waste part is just what the guy thinks. You can't look that one up." Ravi replied with a thinking face. Marisol replied, "wait, so we were fighting about which part?" and then, a minute later, "because I only care about the park part."

Colton looked at the two distinct arguments, one about money that could be counted and one about fun that could not, sitting there in the same sentence like they belonged together. He picked his phone back up and typed: "new rule. If you can check it, link it." Ravi sent a thumbs up. Then a link appeared, from Ravi, to a petition for the pool. "This one you can check," Ravi wrote. "It has zero signatures."

activity: to tell a physical change like melting from a chemical change like rusting or burning
knowledge_domain: to tell a physical change like melting from a chemical change like rusting or burning
fact: A proton has about 1,836 times the mass of an electron, so almost all of an atom's mass is in its nucleus.
story:
Tyler had promised his mom the kitchen table would be clear by six, and it was now 5:15, with the table covered in marbles, peppercorns, toothpicks, and a poster board that still said ATOM in crooked letters. The science fair was tomorrow morning. He had a model to build and, more urgently, a claim to fix, because last week he had told his whole class that burning toast was "basically the same as ice melting, just warmer." Priya had looked at him the way you look at a rodent that has wandered into your lunch bag, and Mr. Okafor had assigned him a demonstration to prove he understood the difference before the fair.

He set up on the counter, since the table was a disaster zone. Two slices of bread went into the toaster: one he would watch melt butter on, and one he would, if necessary, burn. Melting was a physical change, because the stuff was still the same stuff, just softer. Burning was a chemical change, because it turned into something new that smelled terrible and could not be unburned. He remembered his dad's old iron kettle rusting on the porch one whole winter, and how no amount of scrubbing ever brought the shiny metal back. That was the flashback he'd put on the poster, drawn as a sad kettle.

But the model was the real problem. He had used a marble for the proton and a marble for the electron, and something about that had bothered him all afternoon. He found the fact in his science book, in a corner, in small print: a proton has about 1,836 times the mass of an electron. He read it three times. "Eighteen thirty-six," he said to the toaster. His little sister, Mia, wandered in looking for cheese.

"A proton has about 1,836 times the mass of an electron," he told her, pointing at the page. "So almost all of an atom's mass is in the nucleus."

"So your electron-marble is basically a lie," Mia said, and took her cheese elsewhere.

Tyler dumped the marble electron back in the bag and hunted through the junk drawer until he found a single poppy seed. He glued it to a toothpick, spun it far out from the marble nucleus, and stepped back. The atom looked suddenly enormous and mostly empty, like a robust orange with one tiny gnat orbiting it. Then the toaster screamed up burnt, and the second slice came out black and smoking, definitely a chemical change, definitely not reversible. He cracked the window so the kitchen wouldn't smell like a cave where something had gone to hibernate, opened the butter dish for the good slice, and wrote "DEMONSTRATION COMPLETE" on the poster in his most confident handwriting. At 5:58, he carried the whole thing to his room, and the table was clear by six, give or take a poppy seed.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: Growth plates, areas of growing cartilage near the ends of children's bones, are weaker than the bone around them, which is why young athletes have limits on repetitive stress.
story:
Juliette lined up at the free throw line for the third drill in a row, and her knee sent up a small, hot signal, like a match struck under her kneecap. She made the shot anyway. Coach Ruiz blew the whistle and called for layups, twenty of them, and Juliette started to run.

By layup fourteen the match had become a torch. She stopped on the baseline, hands on her knees, and pretended to be catching her breath. Across the gym, Danny from the baseball team sat on the bleachers with his arm wrapped in ice, sulking. "Pitch count," he said when he caught her looking. "Coach says I hit my limit for today." He rolled his eyes. "My arm feels fine."

Juliette had heard Danny's older brother talking last week, something about growth plates, areas of growing cartilage near the ends of kids' bones. The weird part was what he'd said next: the cartilage is weaker than the bone around it. That was why young athletes had limits on repetitive stress, limits that felt pointless because nothing hurt yet. She had tuned most of it out, thinking it was baseball stuff. Now she stood in a gym doing her twentieth layup on a knee that only complained sometimes, and wondered whether the pain was the whole warning or just the part she could see. Maybe the real damage was quiet. The thought seemed to magnify every ache she had ignored since September, including the day she'd jumped rope for an hour on a sore ankle because quitting felt like despair.

She jogged to the sideline. "Coach, my knee's been aching after practice, and it's not going away. Can I sub out of the jumping drills?"

"Smart," Coach Ruiz said. "Ice it."

Danny raised his ice pack toward her like a toast. "Look at us. Bench buddies."

She hadn't solved anything. She still didn't know if she'd been reckless or just tired, and the doctor appointment on Saturday loomed like a full-court press. But when the team ran suicides, she sat, watching, and pressed the ice against her knee until it burned cold.

activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
knowledge_domain: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
fact: Two players can have the same average while one is steady and the other swings between great and terrible games, since an average hides how spread out the results are.
story:
The bus jolted over the pothole by the gym, and Peyton grabbed the seat in front of her before she slid into the aisle. In her backpack was the sign-up sheet for Saturday's three-on-three basketball tournament, and one blank line left: her third teammate. She had until the last stop to decide.

"I still say Dez," said Marcus, leaning over from the next seat. "He's got the same average as Priya. Ten points a game. I did the math twice."

Peyton pulled out her notebook, where she'd copied the numbers from the rec center's weekly sheets. "Same average, but look." She turned the page so he could see. "Priya scored ten, ten, nine, ten, eleven. Every single week. Dez scored twenty-two, then two, then eighteen, then zero, then eight."

Marcus squinted at the columns. Rain had begun to saturate the windows, blurring the parking lots and mailboxes into gray streaks, and he had to tilt the notebook toward the light. "So? They both average ten."

Down the aisle, Dez was holding court near the back, retelling last week's game in a loud voice. "Twenty-two points! It was a siege out there, they double-teamed me all night, and I still dropped twenty-two." A couple of kids laughed and pounded his shoulder. Priya sat quietly by the window, retying her shoelace the way she did before every game, careful and slow.

Peyton frowned at her numbers. The average treated Priya's week and Dez's week the same, but the weeks underneath weren't the same at all. She thought about Saturday. Three games guaranteed, maybe five if they kept winning. She needed somebody she could count on every game, not one brilliant game and then a collapse. She tested the idea on Marcus.

"Okay, forget averages. If I tell you our first game, Priya gives us ten points. Can you promise me Dez does?"

Marcus rubbed the back of his neck. "No. He might give us two. He might give us twenty."

"Right. An average hides how the games are spread out." She tapped the two columns. "Priya's all bunched together. Dez swings between great and terrible."

Marcus was quiet for a second. The bus hissed to a stop and two fifth graders clattered down the steps. "I wanted Dez because he's fun," he admitted. "But you're right, we need steady. Put Priya down."

Peyton wrote the name, then got up and walked back through the swaying aisle. She sat down across from Priya, who looked up, surprised.

"Want to be on our tournament team Saturday?" Peyton asked. "Three games minimum."

Priya's slow smile spread. "I'll be there. Every game."

"I know," said Peyton. "That's why I asked."

Marcus turned around in his seat and held out his fist, and Priya bumped it just as the bus lurched forward into the rain.

activity: to sort rocks as igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic by how they were formed
knowledge_domain: to sort rocks as igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic by how they were formed
fact: Fossils are found almost only in sedimentary rock, because the heat that forms igneous and metamorphic rock usually destroys remains.
story:
Grandpa's creek had yielded exactly zero fossils in three days of searching, which Victoria considered a personal insult. She had a shoebox of rocks on the porch rail, and she spread them out now: speckled ones, banded ones, one gray lump with shiny flecks that looked like someone had spilled glitter into wet concrete.

Grandpa came out with two glasses of lemonade and peered over her shoulder. "Grandma wants to retire that shoebox, by the way. She says it's full of dirt and mystery."

"It's full of specimens," Victoria said. She picked up the glittery one. "This one's igneous, I think. It was melted once, like lava, and then it cooled." The banded one went in a second pile. "Metamorphic. Squished and cooked underground until it got stripes." The third pile was softer rock, layered like a stack of pressed sandwiches. "Sedimentary. Made from mud and sand piling up."

"That's a lot of science for a shoebox," Grandpa said.

She held up her favorite find, a black stone from the creek bend. "I checked this one four times for fossils. Nothing." She had checked the banded one too, and the glittery one, dragging her thumb over every surface like a detective looking for fingerprints. Nothing, nothing, nothing.

Then she turned over a piece of the layered sandwich rock, and there it was: a curl pressed into the stone, small and perfect, like a snail that had signed its name a very long time ago.

"Fossil!" She nearly knocked over the lemonade.

Grandpa leaned in. "How come it's in that one and not the fancy ones you kept checking?"

Victoria lined up the three piles side by side. "The melted kind was too hot, I bet. The squished kind too. Anything living in there would've burned up." She tapped the soft layered pile. "Only these. Fossils are almost only ever in sedimentary rock."

"So the glitter rock is controversial."

"It's a paperweight," Victoria said. She wrapped the fossil in her bandana like it was a visiting ambassador, and carried it inside to show her grandmother.

activity: to find the theme of a novel and back it up with a quotation from the text
knowledge_domain: to find the theme of a novel and back it up with a quotation from the text
fact: In James Hurst's 1960 story The Scarlet Ibis, a storm-blown red bird dies in the family garden, foreshadowing the fate of the fragile boy Doodle.
story:
Autumn had read the last page of The Scarlet Ibis twice, and she still could not say what the book was about in one sentence. Mrs. Ruiz's book club met in the library on Thursdays, and today each member had to state a theme and back it up with a quotation. Autumn's hand was sweating against her notebook.

She assumed everyone else had figured it out already. Marcus was flipping through his copy with a smug little smile, and Priya had three sticky notes bristling from her pages. Autumn had one sticky note, stuck to a page about a red bird. When the storm blew the scarlet ibis into the family's garden and it died, she had felt something tighten in her throat, though she could not say why.

"It's about guilt," Marcus announced. "The narrator's conscience bothers him, so it's about a guilty conscience." He read his quotation in an eloquent, dramatic voice, wobbling his eyebrows at Priya, who snorted so hard she knocked over the pretzel bowl.

Then it was Autumn's turn. She opened to the red bird. "I think it's about fragility," she said. "When the scarlet ibis dies in the garden, it's like the book is telling you something before it happens." She read her quotation about the fallen bird, and her voice came out steadier than she expected. "Doodle is fragile too. And later, in the storm, when the narrator finds him under the tree with his neck bent, it's like the bird all over again." The room went quiet except for the radiator ticking. Priya leaned over and flipped back to the bird scene, her finger moving down the page.

"That's foreshadowing," Priya whispered, tapping the dead red bird. "You found it before me."

Mrs. Ruiz wrote "storm" on the board and underlined it twice. "Notice," she said, "that a storm brings the bird, and a storm takes Doodle."

Autumn copied the word foreshadowing into her notebook, pressing hard enough to dent the next page, and then tore off the corner and folded it into a tiny paper bird.

activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
knowledge_domain: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
fact: Historians still do not know who fired the first shot at Lexington in April 1775; British and colonial witnesses each said the other side fired first.
story:
Carter arrived at Deshawn's house with his backpack clanking, ready for history club, and found everyone arguing before he even got his shoes off. Three kids sat around the kitchen table with two photocopied pages in front of them, and the smell of burned popcorn hung in the air from an earlier disaster nobody would admit to.

"It says right here the British fired first," Priya said, tapping her page. "The colonist witness says so."

Deshawn shook his head. "My page is a British soldier's account, and he swears the colonists fired first. Same morning, April 1775, at Lexington. Somebody's lying."

Carter sat down and pulled both pages toward him. He read them twice, chewing the end of his pencil. Both accounts sounded certain. Both had details, the smell of gun smoke, the shape of the green, the shout of officers. If people on both sides each said the other side fired first, then either one witness lied, or both sides honestly remembered it differently. He wanted to know which, and he thought of a way to check.

"I want to replicate the argument," he said. "Kind of. Priya, you go stand by the sink. Deshawn, stand at the back door. Amelia, you're the shot. Slam the pantry door."

Amelia grinned and slammed it. "Who fired?" Carter asked. Priya pointed at the back door. Deshawn pointed at the sink. Neither had seen the pantry. They tried it again with different positions, and every time, each witness truly believed the other person's side had caused the bang.

"So that's it," Carter said slowly. "Nobody has to be lying." Historians still did not know who fired the first shot at Lexington, because the witnesses from each side each said the other side fired first, and maybe every one of them believed it. The kids sat quietly for a moment, letting that settle.

Deshawn's mom came in with a fresh bowl of popcorn, having noticed the earlier loss from the scorched smell drifting upstairs. "You kids want juice too?" She set down cups without waiting for an answer. Priya slid the biggest cup toward Carter, since he'd missed snack time entirely by reading twice.

"Next meeting," Deshawn said, "we find a case where the two sides actually agree. Something parallel to this one."

"Deal," said Carter, and reached for the popcorn.

activity: to write a five-paragraph persuasive essay with an introduction and a conclusion
knowledge_domain: to write a five-paragraph persuasive essay with an introduction and a conclusion
fact: Naming where a statistic came from, such as the organization that published it, lets readers check it and makes a persuasive essay more believable.
story:
Amelia spread her notebook across the library table and wrote "Five Reasons the Library Should Stay Open Until Eight" at the top of the page. Below it she made her outline: introduction, three reason paragraphs, conclusion. The librarian, Mr. Okafor, had told her class that a persuasive essay was like a court case, and each paragraph had to prove something. Amelia thought that sounded manageable until she sat down and realized she had exactly one fact, which was that some kids couldn't come to the library until after five because of the bus schedule.

Her friend Dev sat down across from her with a stack of books about frogs, because he was doing a report on animals that hibernate. "What's your essay about?" he asked.

"The library should stay open later," Amelia said. "Kids check out forty percent more books when it's open late."

Dev frowned. "Says who?"

"Says me. I made it up. It sounds convincing."

"That's not how it works." Dev turned a page. "If you put a number in there, people want to know where it came from. Like, if I write that wood frogs freeze solid all winter, I have to say the wildlife federation said that, or nobody believes me."

Amelia tapped her pencil. She looked over at the front desk, where Mr. Okafor was stamping returns, and got an idea. She wrote her opening paragraph on a fresh sheet, left out any sources, and walked it over to him. "Mr. Okafor, can you read this and tell me what you think?"

He read it and pointed at her number. "Forty percent more books. Says who?"

Exactly as predicted. Amelia grinned, went back to the table, and found the library's annual report in the reference section, which listed checkout totals by month and hour. The real number was smaller than her made-up one, but it came with a name attached: the report was published by the city library board. She wrote the sentence again with the real figure and added "according to the city library board's annual report," then took it back to the desk.

Mr. Okafor read it and nodded. "Now I can go look that up myself if I want to. That's a competent piece of arguing."

"But my first number was bigger," Amelia said.

"Bigger and useless. The expense of staying open late is real, so your argument has to be real too."

Dev raised his hand without being asked. "Point of order. I changed my mind about frogs. They don't all hibernate. Some just slow down and lurk under mud, being dramatic."

"That's not a point of order," said Amelia.

"It is now," said Dev, and he crossed out a whole paragraph with great satisfaction.

activity: to perform a monologue from a play using pauses and gestures to show emotion
knowledge_domain: to perform a monologue from a play using pauses and gestures to show emotion
fact: A straw man argument misstates an opponent's position as something weaker or sillier, then attacks that version instead of the real one.
story:
The list went up on the community theatre door at four o'clock sharp: showcase auditions, Friday night, one monologue each. Chase had five days to make Director Voss believe he could hold a stage alone, and he'd picked the trickiest speech in the whole script room, a town council scene from an old play called The Long Meeting. The character, a kid named Pip arguing at a council hearing, had a page of lines and zero stage directions printed. Everything, Ms. Voss told him with a wave of her feathered pen, would have to come from his pauses and his hands. "The audience can't hear a comma," she said. "You have to show it."

By Wednesday Chase had the words memorized, but the scene felt flat. In it, Pip stands up and asks the council to shorten the town festival by one day so the park grass can recover. The council president then rises and thunders that Pip obviously wants to cancel the festival forever, shut down the vendors, and erase a hundred years of tradition. The crowd gasps. Pip gets shouted down. Chase ran it again in the empty green room and frowned. Why would the crowd gasp at something Pip never said?

He flipped through the script and found the answer tucked in the playwright's note. Pip's friend whispers a single line: "He's building a straw man argument." Chase read it twice. So that was the game. The president takes Pip's small request, blows it up into something weaker and sillier, a total ban, and then attacks that puffed-up version instead of what Pip actually said. Nobody fights the real Pip. They fight the fake one, because the fake one is easier to beat.

That was the key to performing it. On Thursday, in front of the mirror in the costume closet, Chase made his choice. When the president ranted, Chase froze Pip mid-step and let three full seconds of silence pass, then lifted one hand, slow and steady, like raising a question mark in the air. The pause would tell the audience something was wrong. The gesture would tell them what. He narrated the beat out loud to himself, experimenting, "Pip doesn't argue yet, he just lets them hear it," and the whole speech snapped into focus around that moment.

Friday night, the house lights dimmed and Ms. Voss called his name from the fifth row, tapping her pen against her clipboard. Chase walked to the center mark, planted his feet, and asked for one day, just one. From the wings, the girl playing the president thundered her wild exaggeration about banning the festival forever, and Chase stopped. One beat. Two. Three. His hand rose, slow and unmistakable, and in the dark he heard somebody in the audience whisper, "Oh, she's twisting it." He let the silence stretch one more second, then said Pip's next line, quiet and clear: "That's not what I said." Ms. Voss's pen stopped tapping.

activity: to explain how a citizen can petition a councillor to change a local bylaw
knowledge_domain: to explain how a citizen can petition a councillor to change a local bylaw
fact: Under first-past-the-post, two similar candidates can split their supporters' votes, letting a third candidate win with fewer votes than their combined total.
story:
Dominic had been rehearsing his speech the whole bus ride, muttering "Honourable Councillor Perkins" until the driver told him to knock it off. He clutched his petition, forty-three signatures demanding the repeal of the bylaw that banned scooters from Miller Park, and marched into the town hall, which smelled like coffee and old carpet. His friend Priya squeezed in beside him. "You've got this," she whispered. "You have more stamina than anyone in Grade 6. Remember the read-a-thon?"

That gave Dominic his opening line. When the mayor called for public comments, he shot up his hand so fast his chair squeaked. "Honourable Councillor Perkins," he began, voice cracking only once, "forty-three citizens signed this petition asking you to review Bylaw 12. That's a real petition, with real names, and it's notarized by my mom." He held it up like a trophy. The room chuckled. Councillor Perkins leaned forward, actually interested, which was more than Dominic had dared hope.

Then she asked the question he'd been dreading. "Forty-three signatures, out of how many scooter riders in town?" Dominic froze. He didn't know. "Hundreds," he guessed. "Maybe more." She nodded slowly. "Then why do you think the bylaw passed in the first place? Someone must have wanted it."

That night Dominic lay awake, thinking. He couldn't see the votes, but he could see their shadow. He pulled out his notebook and sketched the last election for park board. Three candidates had run. Ms. Ortiz got 34 percent, Mr. Bell got 33 percent, and Ms. Grant got 33 percent, and Grant won, barely, because she edged out Bell by four votes. But Ortiz and Bell had both campaigned on the exact same promise: more scooter restrictions. Dominic added the numbers twice, then three times, because he didn't believe his own arithmetic. "They had way more votes together," he whispered to his ceiling. "And they still lost."

The next morning he collabed with Priya over cafeteria fries, laying out his notebook like a detective on TV. "It's called first-past-the-post," she said, tapping his page. "My sister taught me. Two similar candidates can split their supporters' votes, and a third candidate wins with fewer votes than both of them combined." Dominic stared at her. "That's it! That's why the bylaw passed. All the anti-scooter people split between Ortiz and Bell, and Grant squeaked through. If either one had dropped out, the other would've won easily." He grinned so wide a fry fell out of his mouth.

At the next town hall meeting, Dominic arrived early with a new petition and a one-page chart, drawn in three colors because he'd decided evidence should be versatile. "Councillor Perkins," he said, "forty-three people signed this, and I can show you why the bylaw only reflects a sliver of the town." She studied his chart, then looked up with a strange smile. "Funny you should mention that election," she said. "I'm Ms. Ortiz."

activity: to tell a physical change like melting from a chemical change like rusting or burning
knowledge_domain: to tell a physical change like melting from a chemical change like rusting or burning
fact: Protons have a positive charge, electrons have a negative charge, and neutrons have no charge at all.
story:
Mason slid a paperclip across the lab table and watched it catch the light. Mr. Okoye had written two lists on the board, one for physical changes like melting ice and bending metal, and one for chemical changes like rusting and burning. The trick, Mason decided, was figuring out whether you could get the old thing back. Melted ice could freeze again. Rusty metal was rusty forever. If only he could see what was actually happening down inside the iron, tiny piece by tiny piece.

His partner Priya had other plans. "We need the atom model for the poster," she said, dumping three bags of beads on the table. "Red, blue, and yellow. I want that blue ribbon at the science fair, so it has to be right." She held up a red bead. "Electrons," she announced, then pointed at a blue one. "Protons."

Mason frowned. "But what's the yellow bead for?"

"The neutrons, obviously."

"Why obviously?"

Priya sighed like he had asked why water was wet. "Protons have a positive charge. Electrons have a negative charge. Neutrons have no charge at all."

"So yellow is nothing?" Mason turned the bead in his fingers. A particle that had no charge at all. It just sat there in the middle of the atom, doing nothing anybody could measure directly. Wait. Could it? His mind jumped back to the rusty paperclip. He couldn't see the iron atoms trading partners with the air, but the rust proved something hidden had happened. The charge rule was the same kind of invisible cause.

He wrote a note and folded it into a paper airplane, flying it across the room to his friend Dario, whose class period transported mail down the hall between labs. The note read: "Burn a small piece of magnesium ribbon for me tomorrow. If it changes to white powder and can't change back, that proves a chemical change happened, even though we can't watch the atoms do it." Dario wrote back one word on the wing: "Deal." Priya glued the yellow beads into the nucleus and held up the finished atom. "Positive, negative, and nothing," she said. "The nothing ones are my favorites."

activity: to revise a draft by cutting weak adjectives and varying sentence length
knowledge_domain: to revise a draft by cutting weak adjectives and varying sentence length
fact: A persuasive essay is stronger when it states the best opposing argument fairly and then answers it; this answer is called a rebuttal.
story:
Rachel's draft was covered in red circles, and she was proud of every single one. "Ten adjectives gone," she told Priya, sliding the paper across the cafeteria table where the writing club met on Tuesdays. "Mr. Okafor called them weak, so I cut them. 'Very big' became 'big.' 'Really exciting' became 'exciting.'" She paused. "Then I cut 'big' and 'exciting' too, just to see what happened. The sentences got shorter. Some of them were three words. Then I made one long sentence on purpose, with a comma, so the rhythm wouldn't be flat."

Priya read the essay, which argued for a later school start time, and frowned. "It's punchy. But my brother read it and said he still didn't believe you, because you never said anything about the buses."

Rachel thought about the buses. She couldn't see her readers, sitting at home, deciding whether to agree with her, but she could picture them, and she could simulate their objections in her head the way she simulated chess moves against her grandfather. Best candidate for the strongest attack: busing schedules would be a mess if school started an hour later. That was the argument that could sink hers.

"That's the thing," Priya said, tapping the margin. "My sister did this for her debate class. You admit the other side has a real point, fairly, and then you answer it. The answer is called a rebuttal."

So Rachel tried it. She wrote that bus schedules really would be harder to change, that drivers might have volatile morning routes that couldn't easily shift, and then she answered it: the district could stagger the three school levels, so buses ran in waves instead of all at once. She hadn't believed it would help. It felt like giving away points. But when Priya read it again, she set the paper down slowly and said, "Okay. Now I'm convinced."

Rachel remembered last month, when she'd refused to change a single word of her poem because revision felt like admitting the first version was a failure. She wasn't sure yet which version of herself had been right. Maybe neither. She picked up her pen and drew one more circle around the word "definitely."

"Cut," she said.

activity: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
knowledge_domain: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
fact: No number of white swans can prove that all swans are white, but seeing a single black swan proves that claim false.
story:
Sofia heard the crash before she even reached the garage, which meant the trash cans were down again. Her little brother Marcus was already crouched behind the workbench, notebook in hand, watching through the window like a detective in a movie.

"It's the Hendersons' dog," Marcus whispered. "Every single trash day. That's my hypothesis." He said the word slowly, the way their science teacher said it, like it was something you could hold. "A testable guess. If I'm right, he'll do it again today."

"You've seen him do it?" Sofia asked.

"No, but the cans are knocked over every trash morning. Nine times now." Marcus flipped through his notebook, nine dates with a crooked checkmark beside each one. "Nine mornings, nine crashes. I'm going to win the science club bet. We took a ballot, and everyone voted that a raccoon was doing it. Everyone except me. If I catch the dog on camera, they have to vote again, and Best Hypothesis is mine."

Sofia pulled the old camcorder off the shelf and wiped the dust from its lens with her sleeve. Nine crashes sounded like proof, but something about it nagged at her. She remembered last summer, when her cousin Deja had insisted that every cat on the block hated water, and how smug she had looked right up until Sofia's cat Mister Pudding leapt straight into the wading pool. Deja had to confess the whole thing afterward, that she'd counted a dozen cats avoiding rain and thought that settled it. "A hundred white swans can't prove all swans are white," Deja had said, staring at the dripping cat, "but one black swan proves that wrong." Sofia hadn't fully understood it then. She was starting to.

"Nine mornings isn't proof," she told Marcus. "It just means the cans fall on trash days. The dog is a guess. So is the raccoon. So is anything until we see it happen."

They set the camcorder on the workbench, aimed at the cans, and waited. The garage smelled like oil and cut wood, and Marcus bounced his knee the whole time. At 6:40 the crash came, louder than usual, and they both lunged for the window.

A garbage truck rumbled past, its mechanical arm swinging wide, clipping the cans and sending them rolling across the driveway. Not a dog, not a raccoon, not anything with legs. Marcus stood frozen with his notebook hanging open, nine checkmarks suddenly meaning nothing at all.

"So I lost the bet," he said finally.

"You lost the bet," Sofia agreed, "but you won the science. Nobody else even tested theirs." She rewound the tape, and the truck swung its arm again on the little screen. Marcus watched it twice, then grabbed his pencil.

"I'm writing this down," he said. "New hypothesis. The arm's too long."

activity: to understand the changes of puberty and why daily showers and deodorant matter
knowledge_domain: to understand the changes of puberty and why daily showers and deodorant matter
fact: Hormones during puberty make the skin's oil glands produce more oil, called sebum, which can clog pores and cause acne.
story:
Emily leaned over the sink and pulled her bangs aside. There, in the mirror, sat a red bump on her chin, and school photos were tomorrow morning.

She thought about her cousin's wedding last summer, when she had skipped showers for three days because the hotel pool "counted." Her skin had erupted afterward, and she had blamed the chlorine. Now she wondered if she had blamed the wrong thing. She ran a finger along her hairline, where her scalp always felt greasy by evening, even on days she washed that morning. The oil seemed to come from somewhere she couldn't see, some place under the skin doing its own work.

Her older sister Maya knocked on the door. "Are you hogging the bathroom again?"

"Maya, come look at this." Emily pointed at her chin. "Where does the stuff even come from? I wash my face."

Maya came in and studied the bump. "It's sebum," she said. "Hormones during puberty make your skin's oil glands pump out more of it, and it clogs your pores." She shrugged. "That's why my face wash has an acne component. It's on the shelf, the blue bottle."

Emily uncapped the blue bottle and sniffed it, sharp and medicinal, like wintergreen. "If oil is the problem, oil should show up somewhere. If I blot my forehead in the morning and after school, I could anticipate when the breakout times are."

So she did. The next morning she pressed a tissue to her forehead, then again after gym class. The morning tissue came away clean; the afternoon one showed a faint shiny smudge, like grease from a slice of nutritious peanut butter toast. The pattern matched her chin getting oilier by evening, too. It wasn't the pool, and it probably wasn't just one skipped shower either, though she still counted that wedding weekend as a strike against her.

Tonight she washed carefully, rolled on deodorant, and set her alarm twenty minutes early so she could wash again before the photographer's flash.

Maya called through the door, "You're still in there?"

"Blotting," Emily said, and held the tissue up to the light.

activity: to understand the changes of puberty and why daily showers and deodorant matter
knowledge_domain: to understand the changes of puberty and why daily showers and deodorant matter
fact: Anxiety disorders are treatable, and cognitive behavioral therapy, which teaches people to notice and change anxious thoughts, is one of the most effective treatments.
story:
The smell arrived on Tuesday, and by Thursday it had claimed the entire row behind Nicolas in science class. Marcus opened the window even though it was January. Ms. Patel didn't say anything, but she did sniff once, pause, and then move the lab demo two tables away, which felt worse than a speech.

The health unit that week covered puberty, and Nicolas learned that sweat glands kick into higher gear around age eleven, and that bacteria, which nobody can see, are what actually make the smell. He turned this over at lunch. An invisible cause, producing a visible, or at least smellable, effect. There was a principle in there somewhere: if the cause was hidden, the fix had to target it anyway, not just the smell. Spraying body spray over it, the way his older cousin did, would be like painting over a leak.

"Testing a theory," he announced that night, and put deodorant, soap, and a clean shirt in his backpack like lab equipment.

The next morning his hands were shaking so much he dropped the deodorant twice in the locker room. Getting changed for gym had become its own problem; his heart hammered whenever it was his turn to be picked for teams, and he'd started pretending he felt sick to avoid it. He told Marcus this while they waited in the gym, in a low voice, expecting mockery.

Marcus shrugged. "That's a thing, you know. Anxiety. I had it about tests last year."

"You? You never worry about anything."

"I worried about everything, I just hid it. My mom took me to a counselor. Anxiety disorders are treatable, and the counselor used cognitive behavioral therapy. That's what it's called. It teaches you to notice anxious thoughts and change them, and she said it's one of the most effective treatments there is."

"Change them how?"

"Like, I'd think, 'I'll fail every question.' She'd have me write that down, then write what actually happened. I usually got a B. My brain couldn't argue with the paper."

Nicolas applied the method right there. His thought: everyone will laugh if I miss the ball. He looked around. Rashad had already tripped over air twice, and nobody had laughed, because they were all too busy being embarrassed themselves. The hammering in his chest dialed itself down a notch.

The principle seemed objective, almost like a rule of the universe: hidden causes, whether bacteria or worried thoughts, still responded to the right tool. The gym teacher, enforcing the everyone-plays rule, pointed at Nicolas. "You're up, serving."

Nicolas tossed the ball, and his serve clipped the net, wobbled, and dropped over. Rashad high-fived him. "See? Invisible bacteria, invisible worries," Nicolas said. "Same principle."

"Did you just compare your brain to armpit germs?"

"Basically."

activity: to sort rocks as igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic by how they were formed
knowledge_domain: to sort rocks as igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic by how they were formed
fact: At new moon, the Moon lies roughly between Earth and the Sun, so its lit side faces away from us and it looks dark.
story:
Landon had one hour before the rock-sorting contest at the science museum ended, and the prize was a summer geology scholarship that would cover the whole field camp. The rules were posted on the wall: sort the twelve mystery rocks into bins marked igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic, by how each rock was formed. His little sister Priya hovered at his elbow, holding the clipboard they had been given.

"Number five," Priya read. "Dark, glassy, with tiny bubbles." Landon turned the rock in his hand. Bubbles meant it had cooled from something molten, he decided, so into the igneous bin it went. The striped one with layers went to sedimentary, and the one that looked squished and swirl-patterned, like a candy cane caught in a press, went to metamorphic. He was halfway through when Priya frowned at the last rock, a pale gray chunk with a pattern of tiny speckles. "This one could violate your whole system," she said. "It's got layers and speckles."

Landon didn't panic. He remembered what an influential scientist in the hall of fame display had written: rocks tell you their story if you look at how they formed, not just how they look.
