He carried the speckled rock to the big wall chart near the astronomy wing, the one he'd read while waiting in line, and compared the speckles to the chart's pictures. Then he grinned. "Cooled from melt. Igneous. The layers fooled me."

"You're sure?" Priya asked.

"New moon sure," Landon said. She looked confused, so he pointed at the ceiling dome, where a moon exhibit glowed. "Last night I couldn't find the Moon anywhere and I thought it vanished. At new moon the Moon lies roughly between Earth and the Sun, so its lit side faces away from us and it looks dark. It was always there. We just couldn't see it." He dropped the last rock into the igneous bin just as the timer buzzed. The judge strolled over, checked the bins, and circled something on her clipboard.

"Twelve for twelve," she said, and stuck a gold star on Priya's clipboard too.

activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
knowledge_domain: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
fact: After about age 40, the lens of the eye loses flexibility and cannot focus up close as well, a condition called presbyopia that reading glasses correct.
story:
Edouard had been waiting for Grandpa's visit all summer, but by the second morning something felt wrong. At breakfast, Grandpa held the cereal box at arm's length and squinted at it like it was a distant bird. When Edouard showed him a comic from his favorite lush, tropical adventure series, Grandpa smiled and handed it back after one glance. "Nice cover," he said, which was a strange thing to say about a comic.

Edouard started watching. At the market café, Grandpa stretched the menu out so far he nearly knocked over the sugar bowl, and he ordered "whatever you're having" instead of reading the specials. In the guest bedroom, the book Grandpa claimed he was reading sat closed on the nightstand while he stared out the window. Edouard had a sinking feeling. Maybe Grandpa didn't actually like comics, or books, or him.

That night Edouard found a clue. Tucked into the suitcase in the guest room was a letter from Grandpa's neighbor back home, and the handwriting was enormous, the letters as big as his thumb. "Your eyes are getting worse," Edouard read, feeling like a spy. "Wear the glasses." There were no glasses anywhere in the room.

He remembered something from last summer, a flashback that rose up sharp and clear. Grandpa threading a fishing hook for him at the lake, holding the line far away and blinking, finally saying, "You do it, Edouard. Your eyes are younger than mine." Edouard had thought Grandpa was just being lazy that day. Now a new idea was forming, and it compressed everything he'd noticed into one tidy thought: Grandpa's eyes worked fine for far away, but not up close. He was hiding it because he didn't want to be a bother.

Edouard tested the idea the next morning. He wrote, in huge letters across a page, WOULD YOU LIKE TO GO TO THE BOOKSTORE? He held it up across the kitchen and watched. Grandpa read it instantly, and his whole face changed.

"Ah," Grandpa said quietly. "You've figured out my secret. After about age forty, the lens of the eye loses flexibility and cannot focus up close as well. It's called presbyopia. My reading glasses correct it, and I left them on the bus." He laughed at himself. "I was too proud to say so."

At the bookstore, Edouard picked out the comic he'd wanted to share and read it aloud in the café, doing all the voices while Grandpa leaned back, listening, easy and happy. When Edouard paused at a cliffhanger, Grandpa's hand shot out and turned the page, quick as a reflex.

"Keep going," Grandpa said. "I have to know if they escape the jungle."

activity: going on a family trip away from home
knowledge_domain: going on a family trip away from home
fact: Most travelers find jet lag harder to adjust to after flying east than after flying west.
story:
Addison pressed her forehead against the airplane window and watched the clouds condense into gray towers below them. Their flight east to Rome had landed two days ago, and she still felt like her body was full of sand. She had fallen asleep at dinner, woken up at four in the morning, and dragged herself through the Colosseum while her little brother, Theo, bounced ahead of her taking pictures of every rock.

"Look at this one," Theo said now, holding up his camera in the Rome airport on their way home. He had one clear objective for the whole trip: get a photo of a pigeon sitting on something ancient. He already had pigeens on a statue, a pigeon on a wall, and, that morning, his prize, a pigeon on a broken column with the Colosseum in the background. "Best trip ever."

Addison couldn't argue, but something bothered her. On the flight out, she had been exhausted. Yet when they landed in Rome, Theo's eyes had gone wide and awake, and even her dad had said he felt strangely fine. It was the days after that had been terrible. On previous trips, flying home, everyone had seemed fine right away. She turned the thought over while they boarded.

Halfway across the Atlantic, she took out her notebook and made two columns. Trip out: flying east, awful afterward. Trip home: flying west. She looked at the columns. Could the direction itself matter? She decided to test it. "Theo," she whispered, "tomorrow, when we land, tell me how you feel. Really tell me."

"Fine, probably," he mumbled into his pillow.

They landed home at six in the evening. Theo ran through baggage claim chasing a plastic water bottle he was kicking like a soccer ball. Addison felt wide awake too, almost too awake, and at midnight she lay in her own bed staring at the ceiling. Her mother passed her door. "Can't sleep either," her mom said. "Funny, coming home is easier."

"It's because we flew west," Addison said. "Going east is the hard one."

Her mom paused in the doorway. "You know, I think you're right."

From down the hall, Theo's voice floated out into the dark. "Does Rome have pigeons at night?"

activity: going to a first sleepover at a friend's house
knowledge_domain: going to a first sleepover at a friend's house
fact: Bright screens late at night can delay sleep, because light, especially blue light, signals the brain to hold back the sleep hormone melatonin.
story:
Cooper had never slept over at anyone's house before, and by eleven o'clock he was starting to worry that he wouldn't sleep at all. Dex's mom had already knocked twice. "Six a.m.," she'd said through the door. "The fishing boat leaves the dock at seven, asleep or not." Now the room was dark except for the glow of Dex's tablet, where they'd been watching video after video since nine.

At midnight Dex shut it off and they lay in their sleeping bags. Cooper stared at the ceiling. His body felt tired, but his brain wouldn't switch off, like a motor still running after the key was turned. Beside him, Dex rolled over for the tenth time.

"I can't fall asleep," Dex whispered. "Me neither," Cooper whispered back. He thought about it. They'd been lying in the dark for half an hour, so being in bed wasn't the problem. What else had they done? He tried to remember something his sister had said once, about light tricking your brain into thinking it's still daytime. It sounded plausible, but he wanted to test it before he trusted it.

"I hypothesize it was the tablet," Cooper said. "All that bright light, right up until we turned it off." Dex sat up. "What's the mechanism, though? How would light keep you awake?" "I don't know exactly. Something about the brain holding back a sleep hormone when it sees light, especially blue light, because it thinks it's daytime. So the hormone never builds up enough to knock us out."

Dex groaned. "Great. So we ruined sleepover night." "Or not," Cooper said. "If light held it back, maybe darkness lets it come back. We just have to stop giving our brains any light at all. No screen, no phone, nothing. Total black." He pulled his sleeping bag over his head like a tent. After a moment, Dex did the same, and the two of them lay there in the warm dark, breathing slowly.

From inside the bag, Dex's voice came muffled. "If this works, we're doing it at every sleepover." Cooper smiled in the darkness and closed his eyes.

activity: spending a surprise snow day at home
knowledge_domain: spending a surprise snow day at home
fact: Fresh snow is mostly trapped air, which makes it a good insulator; some small animals survive winter in tunnels under the snow.
story:
Sophia heard the words "snow day" from the hallway and was out of bed before her alarm finished ringing. By nine she was dragging her red sled up Miller's Hill, where her friend Marcus was already stomping a path along the ridge. He pointed at a long sled with runners he'd borrowed from his cousin. "I'm breaking the hill record today," he said. "Cousin Tyler did the whole slope in twelve seconds. I timed him."

"First you have to help me with something," Sophia said. She had noticed it the day before, when she'd dug into the drift at the bottom of the hill. The deeper she'd gone, the less cold it felt. Today she wanted to test it properly, like the experiments they did in science, except this one was hers. They scooped and packed snow until they had a fort with walls as thick as Sophia was tall, and she hung a thermometer from a stick inside it. Then she tucked a second thermometer into a bush out in the open wind.

While they waited, Marcus scrutinized the snow around the fort, crouched low, frowning. "Look at this," he said. A thin, winding groove ran along the surface of the drift and vanished into it, like a tiny tunnel with a roof of snow. "Something's living under here." They followed the groove, careful not to cave it in, and Sophia remembered something from a winter documentary she'd watched in October, about how fresh snow is mostly trapped air, which makes it a good insulator, and how some small animals survive the whole winter in tunnels under the snow. "That's probably a vole," she said. "The snow is like a blanket over its hallways." Marcus said his grandfather had once shown them a moth larva curled under tree bark in January, and Sophia said that was the same idea: small things hiding in warm pockets while everything above them froze.

They ran back to check the thermometers, and Sophia could hardly keep still while she read them. Inside the fort it was several degrees warmer than out in the wind, and neither of them had done anything but pile up snow. "It works," she said. "It actually works." Then came the twist. From inside the grooved drift came a scrabbling sound, and a gray shape burst out of a hole near their feet, agile as a dart, streaking across the snow and diving into the next drift over. A vole, fat and quick, using its tunnels like a secret highway.

Marcus stood with his sled in both hands, watching the hole. "The snow fort is basically a giant vole tunnel," he said. "That's the best thing I've ever heard." He set the sled at the top of the hill and pointed down the slope. "Twelve seconds. Count them out loud." Sophia planted her boots at the bottom, cupped her hands around her mouth, and shouted, "Three, two, one, go!"

activity: to explain supply and demand using the price of strawberries in summer and winter
knowledge_domain: to explain supply and demand using the price of strawberries in summer and winter
fact: British economist Alfred Marshall popularized the supply-and-demand diagram, with its two crossing curves, in his 1890 book Principles of Economics.
story:
The farm stand smelled of warm dirt and crushed leaves, and Emilie wiped strawberry juice off the counter for the third time that hour. Mr. Ruiz paid her five dollars a morning to stack baskets, make change, and answer questions, but today her math homework sat folded in her back pocket like a stone. She was supposed to draw two lines that crossed like an X and write about why strawberries cost two dollars a basket in June and six dollars in January. The lines themselves she could copy from the book, but she could not figure out who had first dreamed them up, and that question itched at her all morning.

A woman came by near noon, a recent refugee from Syria who had started coming every week with her two small sons. She counted coins carefully, and Emilie noticed she always bought more strawberries in summer, sometimes three baskets, and in winter she walked past them. "In winter they cost too much," the woman said simply, and Emilie felt something click, like a key finding its lock. More berries in summer made the price sink; fewer in winter made it climb. The X shape in her homework was just that idea, drawn.

During her break she asked Mr. Ruiz if she could borrow the shop's old laptop, its porous speaker crackling as it hummed to life. She typed "who made the supply and demand curves famous" and chewed her thumbnail while the page loaded. There it was. A British economist named Alfred Marshall had made the two crossing curves famous in his 1890 book, Principles of Economics. She read the name twice, then copied it onto her homework sheet in careful letters.

"Find what you needed?" Mr. Ruiz asked when she handed back the laptop.

"Alfred Marshall," Emilie said, holding up her paper. "He made my homework famous first." Outside, the strawberry vines flourished in the July heat, heavy with fruit, and she went back to the counter to stack another row of two-dollar baskets.

activity: to find the theme of a novel and back it up with a quotation from the text
knowledge_domain: to find the theme of a novel and back it up with a quotation from the text
fact: In Shakespeare's English, he or she verbs often end in -eth or -th, so doth means does and hath means has.
story:
Matthew slouched at his table in room 12, staring at the photocopied page where Mr. Ruiz had typed the same question three times: What is the theme of the novel? Support your answer with a quotation. Last week Matthew had written "the theme is friendship" and gotten it back with a red circle around nothing, which felt worse than a circle around something wrong. At least a mistake could be diagnosed. This was just empty.

"You have to use the actual text," said Priya, leaning over. "Like, copy a line and connect it."

"I know that," Matthew said, though he did not. Their class novel was an old retelling of Romeo and Juliet, and half of it sounded like a foreign language. He flipped to his marked page and read aloud in a whisper: "'She hath not seen the change of fourteen years.'"

Priya squinted. "She hath not seen the change of fourteen years. What's hath?"

"Beats me. Maybe it's 'hates'?" He tried it. "She hates not seen the change of fourteen years." That collapsed instantly, like a tent with one pole missing. He read further and found "he doth keep the peace" and "what doth it profit a man." Doth kept showing up where a verb belonged. He tested a pattern, the way he tested cheat codes: swap doth for does. "He does keep the peace." That worked. He looked back at hath. If doth meant does, maybe hath meant has. "She has not seen the change of fourteen years." The whole sentence snapped into place.

"That's it," Priya said, writing it down. "So hath means has. That's, like, their word for it."

Matthew's hand shot up before he could talk himself out of it. When Mr. Ruiz called on him, he stood, ears hot, and read the quotation in both versions, the old words and the plain modern English underneath. "The theme is that kids grow up faster than the grown-ups want them to. She hasn't even turned fourteen yet, and the whole story is already happening to her."

Mr. Ruiz didn't smile, but he underlined something on his clipboard, and Priya kicked Matthew's chair leg under the table, twice, which was her way of cheering.

That night Matthew found his father's old copy of Shakespeare on the shelf at home, its cover soft from years of hands. He hadn't known why he'd avoided it before, and he didn't entirely know why he was opening it now, except that last week he'd looked at a page like this and seen a locked door, and today someone had handed him a key. The house smelled like burnt toast from the kitchen, and from downstairs his father called, "You reading that thing?"

"Yeah," Matthew said. "He doth write pretty good."

His father's laugh came through the floorboards.

activity: to shade a sphere with a light source to show highlight, shadow and cast shadow
knowledge_domain: to shade a sphere with a light source to show highlight, shadow and cast shadow
fact: The terminator is the line on a sphere where the lit side turns into the shadow side, the edge where direct light stops reaching.
story:
Victor wanted his grandmother's annual art contest entry to be perfect, mostly because his cousin Priya had won it two years running. At the kitchen table in his grandparents' house, he kept drawing the same beach ball and it kept looking flat, like a sticker of a ball instead of a ball. His grandmother nurtureed his habit of trying again, sliding him a fresh peach and saying that she couldn't help him herself, since she had an allergy to pencils, which was her joke for arthritis. Grandpa, reading in the corner, looked over the top of his glasses and said one thing: "Artists call that line the terminator."

"Like the robot?" Victor said, but Grandpa only shrugged and went back to his book. Terminator. Robots didn't seem to have anything to do with a peach.

Then Victor carried the peach to the window, where the morning sun hit it sideways, and turned it slowly in his fingers. There was a line, curving around the fruit, where the bright gold stopped and the dusky side began. It wasn't a drawn line. Nothing marked it. It was simply the edge where the light stopped reaching, and on the table below, the peach threw a second, darker pool of shadow that stretched away from the sun. He fetched the desk lamp and angled it high, then low, watching the line slide and the cast shadow shorten and stretch like something alive. What if his ball looked flat because he had skipped that line entirely, shading everything softly the same way?

Back at the table, he sharpened his pencil to an acute point and drew the beach ball again, this time finding the terminator first, laying a definite shadow on the far side and a crisp cast shadow beneath it, then gently blending toward a bright spot where the lamp would have been. Grandpa wandered over, peach in hand, and studied the page. "Huh," he said. "Priya's going to hate this." Victor turned the drawing toward the window to check it in better light.

activity: to follow a recipe to bake muffins from start to finish including preheating the oven
knowledge_domain: to follow a recipe to bake muffins from start to finish including preheating the oven
fact: Mise en place is a French cooking term meaning 'putting in place': preparing and measuring every ingredient before you start cooking.
story:
Paisley cracked the first egg into the bowl before she had measured anything else, and by nine thirty the counter looked like a flour bomb had gone off. "The muffins have to be out of the oven by eleven," her friend Ruby reminded her, "because Mr. Delgado, our upstairs tenant, comes down for coffee at eleven sharp, and he judges everything." Paisley raced to the pantry for baking powder, came back, and discovered she'd forgotten to preheat the oven entirely. "The oven's cold as a swimming pool," she groaned. Ruby peeked at the recipe card. "It says preheat first. Four hundred degrees. It also says something weird at the top."

The card read, in Grandma Cruz's handwriting: Mise en place. "It's French," Ruby said, squinting. "It means 'putting in place.' Measuring out every single ingredient before you start cooking." Paisley looked at her lumpy batter, then at the oven, then at the clock. Ten o'clock. If she kept hunting for cinnamon while things sat and oven temperatures climbed, nothing would be done by eleven, and Mr. Delgado would shake his head and call their kitchen impoverished, which was his word for anything missing blueberries.

"We start over," Paisley announced, dumping the batter into the sink with ceremony. "This time I test the French way." She turned the dial to four hundred, then lined up little bowls on the counter like soldiers: flour, sugar, baking powder, salt, oil, milk, one egg. Ruby rinsed blueberries and let them contribute to the cause by plopping them in a cup. "You look like a scientist," Ruby said. "I look like a person who knows where her cinnamon is," Paisley said, holding up the cinnamon like a trophy.

At eleven sharp the muffins came out golden, the tops cracked just right, and Mr. Delgado arrived downstairs sniffing the air like a bear at a picnic basket. He bit into one, chewed, and nodded slowly. "Not impoverished at all," he declared. "Who measured everything in advance?" Paisley raised her hand. "Mise en place," she said. "Second batch's on me," said Mr. Delgado, reaching for a second muffin.

activity: to build a simple circuit with a battery, a switch and a bulb and explain why it lights
knowledge_domain: to build a simple circuit with a battery, a switch and a bulb and explain why it lights
fact: For a metal wire at constant temperature, a graph of voltage against current is a straight line through zero, and its slope is the resistance.
story:
Elena spread her battery, bulb, switch and coiled wire across the picnic table at the edge of the skate park, because her brother Tomas refused to skip practice and she refused to fail Monday's science demonstration. She clipped the wire to the battery, flipped the switch, and the bulb stayed dark. She unclipped and reclipped every connection, but it was like arguing with the ramp: the same input, the same nothing. The skaters had started to migrate to the shaded half-pipe as the tropical afternoon heat pressed down, and a plague of gnats circled her table, but she kept working.

She took the bulb off and clipped the wire straight to a small meter instead. If current was flowing, the needle would move even though she could not see current itself. It did not move. "So the battery's fine or it's not," she said to herself, "but something between here and here is broken." She tested each piece of wire by touching its ends to the meter until one stretch, cracked where skaters had rolled over it, gave nothing at all. She replaced it, flipped the switch, and the bulb glowed. When her friend Dara rolled up, Elena held the lit bulb and said, "It lights because the switch closes the path, so current goes around the whole loop through the filament."

A text arrived from Tomas, on the far ramp: "Coach says graph beats guessing. Did you try the meter trick or just stare at it?" Elena typed back: "Meter trick. Found a dead wire. Also took five readings of voltage and current with the good wire, like the handbook said."

She plotted the five points on graph paper, voltage up the side, current along the bottom. The points fell into a straight line, and when she extended it backward with her ruler, it passed through zero, where no voltage meant no current. The line climbed steeply, which matched the way her bulb pushed back against the flow. Dara leaned over her shoulder and read the page. "That line means something?" Elena tapped the slope with her pencil and said, "The slope is the resistance." Dara nodded slowly, spun her board up onto the table, and said, "Show me the bulb again."
